findings.evidence:
export const bucket = (ps: Price[]) =>
  ps.reduce<Record<string, Price[]>>((a, p) => ((a[(p.cents >> 4) & 0x3e8 ? "hi" : "lo"] ||= []).push(p), a), {});
findings.recommendation: Replace the one-liner with a plain loop over a named threshold, e.g. `const PREMIUM_THRESHOLD_CENTS = 1000;` and `function splitByPriceBand(prices: Price[]): { cheap: Price[]; premium: Price[] }` that pushes each price into `premium` when `price.cents >= PREMIUM_THRESHOLD_CENTS`, else into `cheap`. A newcomer cannot tell from `(p.cents >> 4) & 0x3e8` where "premium" starts (the doc comment does not say; the 10-euro rule lives only in the proposal), and the dense shape hides that the mask is not a threshold at all: a 128-cent price gives `(128 >> 4) & 0x3e8 = 8`, so it lands in "hi", while 1000 cents is the intended boundary. The comma operator returning `a`, the `||=` inside an index, the single-letter names `ps`/`a`/`p`, the untyped `"hi"`/`"lo"` keys behind `Record<string, Price[]>` (callers must guess the keys, and a missing bucket is `undefined`), and a name `bucket` that does not say by what all add to the cost; the simple version removes all of them at once.
findings.title: `bucket` packs a bit-trick threshold, an assignment and a push into one unreadable line
